t: Check If String Is Transformable With Substring Sort Operations - Smaller Digits Are Immovable Roadblocks
o:
## Understanding the problem

We may repeatedly pick any substring of `s` and sort it in ascending order, and must decide whether `t` is reachable. The operation obeys one structural law: take digits e < d; if e currently sits somewhere to the left of d, no sequence of sorts can ever move d left of that occurrence of e, because any sort containing both places e first. A smaller digit on the left is therefore a permanent roadblock.

The strategy follows: build `t` greedily from the left. For the digit d demanded at the current position, grab the leftmost still-unconsumed copy of d in `s` - it faces the fewest roadblocks, and equal copies are interchangeable - and demand that no remaining smaller digit sit before it.

In `84532` -> `34852` every step passes that test (sort `53` into `35`, then `843` into `348`). In `34521` -> `23415` it likewise succeeds. In `12345` -> `12435` the `3` still stands left of the `4` we want to place first, so the answer is false.

Lengths up to 100000 rule out any search over arrangements; a digit-by-digit greedy backed by ten position buckets runs in linear time.
k: Invariant: for digits e < d their relative order (e before d) can never flip, so any unconsumed smaller digit left of your chosen placement makes the attempt impossible.
Greedily consume the leftmost remaining copy of the demanded digit - equal digits are interchangeable and this copy has the fewest roadblocks ahead of it.
Ten FIFO position lists with one head pointer per digit give an O(n) solution with a constant factor of ten.

a.i: Treat every arrangement of the multiset of digits as a graph node, connect states reachable through one substring sort, and run BFS from s hunting for t. The model is completely faithful to the operation and always terminates since the state space is finite, but distinct arrangements grow combinatorially, so this only serves as a mental model or works on toy strings. A quick multiset equality pre-check prunes hopeless cases instantly.
s: If sorted(s) differs from sorted(t), return false immediately.
Start BFS from s, remembering visited states in a set.
Expand a state by sorting each substring i..j and enqueueing unseen results.
Return true the moment t appears; return false when the queue drains.
a.t: Exponential - the reachable state space can be factorial in n.
a.sp: Exponential - every visited arrangement is memorized.

a.n: Approach 2: Ten Position Queues and a Greedy Match
a.i: Bucket the indices of s by digit into ten ascending lists. Scan t left to right; for the demanded digit d, peek the leftmost unconsumed index i of d. If some strictly smaller digit still has an unconsumed index before i, that digit is stranded left of i forever and we return false; otherwise consume i and continue. Correctness rests directly on the roadblock invariant, and each index enters and leaves its bucket exactly once.
s: Build pos[d] as the ascending list of indices where digit d occurs in s.
Keep one head pointer per digit marking consumed entries.
For each character d of t: fail if pos[d] is exhausted; let i be its front element.
Fail if any smaller digit's front index is less than i.
Advance the head of pos[d]; after processing all of t, return true.
a.t: O(n) - every index is appended and consumed once; the 10-digit scan is constant work.

w: Present the invariant first - a smaller digit never yields its place - then derive the queue greedy from it; that narrative arc is what gets graded. Pitfalls: picking a non-leftmost copy of the demanded digit (always take the leftmost), using <= instead of strict less-than against smaller fronts (equal indices cannot coexist across different digits, but keep the comparison strict for clarity), and skipping the implicit check that t uses only digits present in s. Edge cases: s equals t, single-character strings, and t demanding a digit absent from s. Likely follow-ups: descending-sort operations (mirror the roadblock logic), or computing the minimum number of operations.
